question: If I'm held in jail awaiting trial, how long can I be held before I must be indicted and tried, and what happens if that deadline passes?

gold_sections.why: Subsection (h): a person detained under (b) goes on an expedited calendar and, consistent with the sound administration of justice, must be indicted within 90 days and have trial commence within 100 days; extensions of up to 45 days each on the government's petition for good cause; indictment at least 10 days before a new trial date; when the clock starts (latest of listed events); excluded periods; after 100 days (plus extensions) the person must be treated under 23-1321(a) unless trial is in progress or delay came from timely motions (not continuances) or the defendant's request. Also (d)(1): the detention hearing is held at first appearance, continuances of up to 5 days (defense) or 3 days (government) absent good cause.

Separate outer limit: if a person committed or held to bail to await the grand jury is not indicted (or the charge ignored) within nine months, the prosecution is deemed abandoned and the person is set free or bail discharged, unless the court enlarges the time for good cause shown in writing with notice.

What being 'treated in accordance with § 23-1321(a)' means: the general pretrial-release order (personal recognizance/unsecured bond, release on conditions, temporary detention, or detention under 23-1322(b)); it also routes first- and second-degree murder and assault with intent to kill while armed to 23-1325.

Detention of persons charged with first- or second-degree murder or assault with intent to kill while armed is ordered under this section, which contains no indictment or trial deadline and does not incorporate 23-1322(h).
(b)(3): 23-1322(d) and (h) apply to revocation-of-release detention for violating release conditions, so the same 90/100-day clock applies.
(d): 23-1322(h) applies to pretrial detention of an addict charged with a crime of violence.

Which cases need an indictment: offenses punishable by more than one year must be prosecuted by indictment unless the defendant waives it; other offenses may proceed by information, so the indictment deadline matters mainly in felony cases.

answer:
If a judge orders you detained before trial under 23-1322(b), your case goes on an expedited calendar [N3]. Consistent with the sound administration of justice, you must be indicted within 90 days [N1] and your trial must begin within 100 days [N2]. The clock usually starts when you are first ordered detained after arrest, and restarts after events like a mistrial [N7]. Interlocutory appeals, competency exams or incompetency, and time you are unavailable do not count [N8].

The prosecutor may seek extensions of up to 45 days each, with the judge's approval [N4], only for good cause such as due diligence and materiality, and only for the time needed [N5]. The indictment must then come at least 10 days before the new trial date [N6].

When the 100 days plus extensions run out, you must be handled under the ordinary release law, 23-1321(a) [N9], whose options include release on personal recognizance or conditions [N11], unless trial has started or the delay came from timely motions (not continuance requests) or your own request [N10]. It does not say the charges are dismissed [N9].

Separately, if you are jailed or bailed awaiting a grand jury that takes no action within nine months, the prosecution is treated as abandoned and you must be freed or your bail discharged [N12], unless the court extends it for good cause shown in writing, with notice to you [N13]. The same clock covers detention for violating release conditions [N15]; murder and assault-with-intent-to-kill-while-armed detentions fall under a different section [N14].

out_of_corpus.what: The constitutional speedy-trial right (Sixth Amendment, Barker v. Wingo balancing test), whose remedy for a violation is dismissal of the charges; it applies to every defendant, detained or not, and is not in the D.C. Code.
out_of_corpus.where: U.S. Constitution, Sixth Amendment, and U.S. Supreme Court and D.C. Court of Appeals case law

out_of_corpus.what: Dismissal for unnecessary delay in presenting a charge to a grand jury, filing an information, or bringing a defendant to trial; time computation and preliminary-hearing timing.
out_of_corpus.where: D.C. Superior Court Rules of Criminal Procedure (Rule 48(b), Rule 45, Rule 5.1)

out_of_corpus.what: Cases prosecuted in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia (federal charges) follow the federal Speedy Trial Act, not D.C. Code 23-1322(h).
How courts read 23-1322(h)(3) (whether release must follow, and whether the 100-day rule reaches 23-1325 murder detentions) is settled by D.C. Court of Appeals decisions, not the statute text.
out_of_corpus.where: D.C. Court of Appeals case law

version_flags: 23-1322(h)(1)'s extension limit 'not to exceed 45 days each' was inserted by D.C. Law 25-175 (Secure DC Omnibus Amendment Act of 2024) section 30(f)(3), which struck 'not to exceed 20 days each'. Under section 8(b)(2) of D.C. Law 26-52 (Oct. 28, 2025) the section 30(f) amendments expire December 31, 2026, after which the extension limit reverts to 20 days each (verified against the D.C. Council's code site and the enacted text of D.C. Law 25-175). In force on 2026-10-10: 45 days.

The corpus copy of 23-1322 notes that it includes temporary legislation expiring September 11, 2026 (D.C. Law 26-81, Peace DC Omnibus Temporary Amendment Act of 2025, Jan. 29, 2026). That temporary act has expired, but its relevant effect (the December 31, 2026 sunset of the Secure DC amendments) is also provided by the permanent D.C. Law 26-52, and the D.C. Council's current text of (h) is unchanged; the quoted clock provisions are in force as of 2026-10-10.

The corpus note says 'section 30(k) of D.C. Law 25-175' amendments expire December 31, 2026, while the code's Expiration of Law note refers to section 30(f); either way the Secure DC amendments to 23-1322 (the 45-day extension, the (c)(9) crime-of-violence presumption, the (f)(3) written-reasons requirement) sunset on December 31, 2026.
notes: Independent second draft. The D.C. Code has no general speedy-trial statute for people on release; the statutory clocks are tied to pretrial detention (23-1322(h), applied to 23-1323 and 23-1329 detentions) plus the nine-month grand jury rule (23-102). The 23-1322(h)(3) remedy is treatment under the ordinary release statute, not dismissal; dismissal for delay comes from the Constitution or Superior Court Rule 48(b). 23-1325 (murder 1 and 2, AWIKWA) detentions are not tied to the statutory 100-day clock by the text. Excluded from gold: 24-801 Interstate Agreement on Detainers (180 days after a prisoner's request / 120 days after arrival, dismissal with prejudice) because it covers people already serving a sentence in another jurisdiction, not pretrial jail detainees; juvenile detention time limits in Title 16 chapter 23; 23-1322(a) 5-day temporary hold of people on release/probation/parole and 23-1322(d)(1) hearing continuances (up to 5 days on the defendant's motion, 3 days on the government's, absent good cause), which concern the initial hold rather than the indictment/trial deadline.
